title: Matrix Inverse
body:
The **inverse** of a square [[Matrix]] $A$ is the matrix $A^{-1}$ with

$$
AA^{-1} = A^{-1}A = I
$$

It is the closest thing matrix algebra has to division, and the gap between "closest thing" and
"division" is where the content is: **not every non-zero matrix has one**. Compare with real
numbers, where every $x \neq 0$ has a reciprocal. A matrix can be full of non-zero entries and
still be **singular** (non-invertible).

Note that $A$ must be square for the equation above to even typecheck, and that the two-sided
condition is automatic: for square matrices, a one-sided inverse is always the inverse.

**What if it is not square, or is singular?** That question is not answered here. The
[[Pseudoinverse]] in [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] answers it: $A^+$ exists for
every matrix and returns the exact solution, the [[Least Squares]] fit, or the smallest solution,
depending on what the system admits.

## When it exists

$A^{-1}$ exists exactly when $\det A \neq 0$. For a $2 \times 2$ that is a formula you should
know cold:

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}
\implies
A^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix}
$$

Swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by the [[Determinant]]. The determinant is in
the denominator, which is the whole story: $\det A = 0$ means dividing by zero, and that is
what singular means.

That single condition has a long list of equivalent phrasings, and the course will use them
interchangeably. For a square $A$, these all say the same thing:

| $A$ is invertible | $A$ is singular |
|---|---|
| $\det A \neq 0$ | $\det A = 0$ |
| $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has exactly one solution for every $\mathbf{b}$ | zero or infinitely many, depending on $\mathbf{b}$ |
| $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ only for $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ | non-trivial solutions exist |
| the columns are [[Linear Dependence\|linearly independent]] | the columns are dependent |
| the columns form a [[Basis]] of $\mathbb{R}^n$ | they span something smaller |
| $A$ reduces to $I$ | reduction leaves a zero row |
| rank is $n$ | rank $< n$, [[Kernel and Range\|kernel]] is non-trivial |
| $0$ is not an [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors\|eigenvalue]] | $0$ is an eigenvalue |

**This table is the spine of the course.** Almost every "show that" question in the first half
is really asking you to walk from one row of it to another.

## Computing it: reduce $[\,A \mid I\,]$

The practical method, and the only one worth using past $2 \times 2$. Write $A$ and $I$ side by
side, then run [[Gaussian Elimination]] until the left half is $I$. Whatever the right half has
become is $A^{-1}$:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 3 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\;\longrightarrow\;
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & 2 \end{array}\right]
$$

so $A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -5 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$. Check it against the
$2 \times 2$ formula: $\det A = 6 - 5 = 1$, and the swap-and-negate gives the same thing.

Why it works: each row operation is an elementary matrix, so reducing $A$ to $I$ means
$E_k \cdots E_1 A = I$, which makes the product $E_k \cdots E_1$ equal to $A^{-1}$. Applying the
same operations to $I$ builds exactly that product. See [[Gaussian Elimination]] for the
elementary-matrix argument.

**If the left half cannot be reduced to $I$**, a zero row appears and $A$ is singular. The
method tells you invertibility and the inverse in one pass.

## The adjoint formula

$$
A^{-1} = \frac{1}{\det A}\,\text{adj}(A)
$$

where $\text{adj}(A)$ is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors. It is the $2 \times 2$
formula generalised, and it is how the general result gets *proved*. It is not how you compute:
it needs $n^2$ determinants of $(n-1) \times (n-1)$ matrices, against $O(n^3)$ for row
reduction. Same relationship as [[Cramer's Rule]] versus elimination.

## Properties

$$
(A^{-1})^{-1} = A, \qquad (AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}, \qquad (A^T)^{-1} = (A^{-1})^T
$$

$$
(cA)^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{c}A^{-1}, \qquad \det(A^{-1}) = \frac{1}{\det A}
$$

**The order reverses in the product rule**, same as with the transpose in [[Matrix]]. Undoing
"put on socks, then shoes" means taking off shoes first.

## Do not solve systems with it

$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ gives $\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$, which is a true statement and
a bad algorithm. Computing $A^{-1}$ and then multiplying costs more than running
[[Gaussian Elimination]] directly on the augmented system, and it loses more precision to
rounding. The inverse is for theory and for algebraic rearrangement; elimination is for
answers. That distinction between "the formula exists" and "the formula is how you compute"
runs through this whole course.

## Related

- [[Determinant]] decides existence
- [[Gaussian Elimination]] computes it
- [[Linear Transformation]]: $A^{-1}$ is the inverse map, and it exists exactly when the
  transformation is one-to-one and onto
- [[Diagonalization]] writes $A = PDP^{-1}$, so it needs $P$ invertible
